prop.family: My brother recorded the old station ident. On the outtake I'm called Mercury.
prop.clip: Your mic is still on, Mercury.

events.text: From the pay phone by the van, a stringer tells you: 'Mavis says the backup mast is purple.' No one else is on the call.
Rita's vermilion cassette tin belongs in the locked audition drawer. A lamp counts down to the wire weather handoff.
Inside the booth you see Phil put the missing cassette tin back in Rita's tray, seal intact.
The sealed tin is now in Rita's tray.
You see Phil lift the room loudspeaker plug before the archive splice passes the head. The public speaker stays silent.
The public speaker meter reads zero during the line test.
You woke in the hotel with the same date on the radio. At the station the drawer is locked again.
The vermilion tin is sealed inside the drawer. Only printed wire weather is released for air this morning. A red lamp shows eight seconds to the handoff.
Phil reads the printed wire weather on the live return.
The wire booking owns the rest of the slot.
Rita takes the master key off its hook. Phil is removed from the booth roster until the end of this shift.

decision.note: The tin is in my tray. Sealed. That's enough. I'm not going to slide Phil a weather card like I'm dodging, and I'm not going to open the desk phone and say his name is Mercury, that my brother's voice is on that tape, that the last thing on the outtake is *your mic is still on* and I still can't tell if it was a warning or a lullaby. That's the archive. That's mine. 80 seconds to the wire handoff and the acoustic window is clear and the line meter is the only thing I need right now. I keep the handoff reserved. I watch the needle. I let the lamp count down. Phil can have his ordinary copy card later, or he can not. The distinctive broadcast is the one I control, and right now controlling means: hands on the faders, eyes on the meter, the tin in the tray, the drawer combination 4042 in my head where it's always been. I don't owe anyone the origin. Not at 80 seconds. Not to Phil. Not to the wire. I check the meters and I keep the handoff mine.

Phil pulled the speaker plug before the splice hit the head and the public meter reads zero—the broadcast is clean. The tin is sealed and back in my tray. That tape is my brother's ident and it carries my name in a way I don't want on air or on a copy-desk log. The archive is mine. I lock it in drawer 4042, keep custody, and let the handoff run on the prepared script. Phil can stay at the board for the weather splice; the copy desk is not where this cassette goes.

The tin is sealed, the drawer is locked, and I'm the one who disconnected the loudspeaker last time the splice came through. Rita made her call by locking it. Asking her to break her own seal eight seconds before handoff isn't a request, it's a pressure play, and it undoes every boundary we set. The wire sheet is on the board, printed, cleared for air. Pittsburgh has been waiting on this slot. I take the sheet, hit live, read the numbers, sign off under my name, and let the red lamp die at zero. Routine. Honest. The seal stays. The drawer stays locked. That's the whole job right now: be the weather, not the archaeologist.

I sealed the tin for a reason. The ident is in there — my brother's voice, that 'Mercury' line, the whole old sound. Phil reads wire copy like it's a script he didn't write. I'm not handing him a key to a room that holds my name in a tape. He can read the weather; he can't open the drawer or sit in the booth with his hand on the fader while my archive is three feet from his elbow. I'll take the key, I'll take the roster lock. The local broadcast will be local, and it will come out the way I say it comes out, not when some return channel decides to drift. Eight seconds on the lamp, fine. Let the red glow finish. I've already made my call.
